docs.title: Project m68k
docs.text:
Run 68040 software (NeXTSTEP, Mac OS, Linux/m68k) on an out-of-order core derived from superdupersparc. The core executes only a micro-op ISA, uisa; 68k instructions reach it two ways:

  • PLA path. Common 68k instructions are length-decoded in hardware and translated by PLAs directly into internal uops.
  • Millicode path. Everything else (complex addressing modes, MOVEM, bitfields, BCD, exceptions, MMU and cache control, floating point) jumps to millicode: ordinary uisa code in hidden memory, written in a C subset and compiled by our own compiler, ucc.

On a NeXTSTEP 2.2 boot to the desktop, about 95% of executed 68k instructions take the PLA path (see PLA flow coverage).

docs.title: The core
docs.text:
The out-of-order core that runs uisa is derived from superdupersparc, an out-of-order SPARC V8 core (itself forked from r9999). It is a 32-bit renamed machine with flags, and it executes only the uisa micro-op ISA: its decoder (decode_uisa.sv), ALU (uisa_alu.sv) and guest-semantic ops (uisa_gop.sv) are built from the tables uisa generates from spec/uisa.yaml, and the FPU is the core's double-precision unit, which uisa's FP extension exposes to millicode.

The PLA translation of common 68k instructions and the millicode for the rest are documented in the uisa reference.

Note

The core's source is not public yet.

docs.title: q800sim
docs.text: A functional Macintosh Quadra 800 (68040) full-system simulator: a plain, readable 68040 interpreter meant to be the golden reference for the uisa micro-engine and its RTL, plus the Quadra 800 machine around it. The address map and device behavior follow qemu's q800 machine (reimplemented, not copied), so runs can be diffed against qemu-system-m68k -M q800.

docs.title: What it models
docs.text:
• CPU: the 68040 integer instruction set, the 68040 MMU (table walk, transparent translation, PTEST), exceptions with 68040 frames, interrupts, STOP, trace.
  • FPU: the 68881 instruction set, with the arithmetic in SoftFloat-3 binary64 and the 68881's NaN and underflow rules. This is the reference for uisa's FP extension.
  • Machine: RAM, ROM, VIA1/VIA2, the SCC console, the 53C96 ESP SCSI controller with disk and CD-ROM targets, SONIC Ethernet with a user-mode NAT backend, direct Linux boot, checkpoints.

docs.title: Two execution engines
docs.text:
--engine interp (the default) runs the 68040 interpreter. --engine uisa runs guest instructions as uisa code instead: the PLA micro-op flows, the MOVEM sequencer and millicode, from a uisa checkout. uisa's loads go through the simulator's MMU and bus, and its exceptions are taken in uisa millicode.

--uisa-check checks every instruction uisa runs against the interpreter before committing it (registers, SR, PC, control registers and the bytes stored), so a full OS boot doubles as a uisa co-simulation.

Note

q800sim's source is not public yet.

docs.title: uisa
docs.text:
uisa is the micro-op ISA the core executes: a clean 32-bit RISC base (fixed 32-bit instructions, load/store, three-operand ALU ops, compare-and-branch) plus the 68k's semantics as first-class operations (sized operands, the five flags with X split out, BCD, rotate through X, address spaces with function codes), so neither the PLA nor the compiler has to emulate them with long sequences. Nothing implicit is left for renaming to undo: partial register writes, partial flag writes and data-dependent register numbers are all visible at the instruction level.

Everything is machine-readable. spec/uisa.yaml is the only definition of the ISA; the decoders, the ISS, the assembler and the reference chapters of the manual are generated from it.

docs.title: uisa: a micro-ISA for a 68040 micro-engine
docs.text: Status: draft 0.1. This document has two parts. The first part (this chapter) is hand-written rationale. The second part, Reference, is generated from spec/uisa.yaml, which is the only place the ISA is defined.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
Run 68040 software, NeXTSTEP in particular, on an out-of-order core derived from superdupersparc. The core is a 32-bit renamed machine with flags; it executes only this micro-ISA. Guest instructions reach it two ways:

  • PLA path. Common 68k instructions are length-decoded in hardware and translated by PLAs directly into internal uops. Those uops never have an encoding; they use the same operations described here.
  • Millicode path. Everything else (complex addressing modes, MOVEM, bitfields, BCD, exceptions, MMU and cache control, floating point) jumps to millicode: ordinary micro-ISA code stored in hidden memory, written in a C subset and compiled by our own compiler.

Bring-up starts with software decode: a millicode interpreter fetches guest instruction bytes with guest-program-space loads and dispatches on the opword. The PLA path is then added for the instructions profiles say matter.

docs.title: Design principles
docs.text:
1. A clean RISC base. Fixed 32-bit instructions, load/store, three-operand ALU ops, no delay slots, no register windows, no condition codes on the base ops. Millicode's own control flow uses compare-and-branch.
  2. Guest semantics as explicit operations. Everything the 68k does that a RISC does not (sized operands, the five flags, X, sticky Z, BCD, rotate through X, address spaces with function codes) is a first-class operation, so neither the PLA nor the compiler emulates it with long sequences.
  3. Nothing implicit that renaming has to undo. Partial register writes, partial flag writes and data-dependent register numbers each cost a source operand or a serialization in a renamed machine. The ISA makes each of those visible at the instruction level (merge forms, the split X/NZVC flag resources, rdg/wrg) so the hardware never discovers them late.
  4. Everything machine-readable. Decoders, the ISS, the assembler and the reference chapters of this document are generated from one YAML file.

docs.title: Register namespace
docs.text:
Register specifiers are 6 bits. x0-x31 belong to millicode (x0 is zero); the guest's D0-D7, A0-A7, PC and SR system byte have their own architectural indices. This keeps all 31 usable x registers available to millicode, which is stackless: a handler whose live values exceed 31 registers fails to compile rather than spilling. Guest registers are reachable from every instruction, so the PLA's uops and millicode name them the same way.

A guest register whose number is only known at run time (an extension-word index register, MOVEM, the Dr:Dq pair of 64-bit multiply/divide) goes through rdg/wrg. Those serialize at rename, so they are expected to be rare. Per-opword handler specialization keeps most register numbers static.

docs.title: Flags
docs.text:
The 68k flags are two renamed resources: NZVC and X. Splitting X out means the many instructions that leave X alone (CMP, the logical ops, MOVE, rotates) do not depend on whichever older instruction last wrote X. Every flag-writing op writes all of NZVC, so NZVC never needs a merge. Ops that use X or sticky Z (ADDX, SUBX, NEGX, ROXL/ROXR, ABCD/SBCD/NBCD) read the old flags explicitly, and so do shifts, because a zero shift count leaves X unchanged.

Every guest op has a variant (.nf) that writes no flags. Most 68k flag results are overwritten before anything reads them, so the PLA and the compiler emit .nf whenever the flags are dead.

A third renamed 1-bit resource, u, is a millicode-private predicate. It is never guest-visible: it is not in the CCR layout (rdccr/wrccr do not touch it) and is not saved or restored, since millicode is not interruptible and u is dead at the end of a routine. Probes write it and conditional loads and stores read it (see below).

docs.title: Sized operations
docs.text:
A renamed machine always allocates a new physical register for the destination. A byte or word operation must therefore copy the upper bits of the old destination into the new one: the merge is unavoidable. The ISA makes it explicit:

  • add.8 d0, d1 is two-address: the old destination arrives on the rs1 port (rs1 must equal rd), the operation runs at 8 bits, flags are taken at bit 7, and the result is merged into the low byte. One instruction, two register reads, no third port.
  • add.8z x5, x6, x7 is the zero-fill form for millicode temporaries whose upper bits are dead. It does not read the old destination, so it does not wait for whatever last wrote that register.
  • add.32 is ordinary three-address.

Sized ops operate on the low n bits of their sources, so right shifts, rotates and rotates through X need no separate extension. Multiply and divide by word produce full 32-bit results (mulu.16, divu.16), matching the 68k.

docs.title: Memory and address spaces
docs.text:
All memory is big-endian. Each load and store names an address space: hidden (physical, untranslated: millicode, its data, devices), guest data, guest program, or guest alternate (function code from SFC/DFC, for MOVES). The guest MMU can never produce a hidden address. Guest accesses may be misaligned; hardware may split them or take an invisible millicode assist.

CAS has its own operation, cas.*, a compare-and-swap like SPARC's CASA: it stores only if the operand equals the compare value and always returns the old operand, so CAS is a short PLA flow with nothing conditional. TAS and CAS2 use locked sequences: ldl.* begins one, stu.* or unlock ends it. All of these execute non-speculatively at the head of the ROB. The machine is single-core, so locking only has to exclude DMA.

Stores can write back their base register: st.<w>.pre stores to rs1 + imm and sets rd to that address, st.<w>.post stores to rs1 and sets rd to rs1 + imm. rd is tied to rs1, so each is two register reads and one result, like the sized merge forms. gpushr is the call-specific version: it stores the return address (the guest instruction's address plus an immediate, known at decode) to a7 - 4 and writes back a7. These are ordinary speculative stores whose register result is ready at address generation, not atomics executed at the head of the ROB. They turn pushes, -(An)/(An)+ destinations, LINK, PEA, BSR and JSR into one or two micro-ops. Loads get no writeback form: a post-increment load would need two results.

probe.r/probe.w translate without accessing and return a status instead of faulting. They build PTEST and let millicode check every address it will touch before it changes any guest state.

For accesses with side effects (uncached device registers), checking is not enough: the accesses themselves must not issue until every probe has succeeded, and a branch on the probe results would be predicted around. So the ordering is a data dependence instead, as in speculative-load hardening. probe.r.us/probe.w.us also set the predicate u to "the probed access would succeed"; the .ua forms AND their result into u. The conditional loads and stores ld.c.*, st.c.* and stu.c.* read u: with u set they are exactly the plain access; with u clear they make no access at all (no translation, no fault), a load returns 0 and a store writes nothing (stu.c still ends the locked sequence). b.u/b.nu branch on u, to the fault path once the accesses are done:

probe.r.us.gd  x5, 0(a0)     ; x5 = MMUSR; u = the read would succeed
probe.r.ua.gd  x6, 0(a1)     ; u &= ok
ld.c.32.gd     x11, 0(a0)    ; if u: load; else x11 = 0, no access
st.c.32.gd     x13, 0(a2)    ; if u: store; else nothing
b.nu           fault

docs.title: Millicode rules
docs.text:
1. Stackless. No memory stack and no spilling. Calls use a hardware return stack (call/ret), depth set by call_stack_depth; overflow is an internal millicode fault. The compiler allocates registers across the whole call graph, which is acyclic because recursion is not allowed. Explicit scratch storage in hidden memory is allowed for state that is genuinely larger than the register file (MOVEM, exception frames, FSAVE).
  2. Faults before commits. A guest-space access can fault, and a fault restarts the guest instruction from the beginning. Millicode therefore performs (or probes) every access that can fault before its first write to guest state. The compiler checks this on its SSA form. PLA flows are short enough to retire atomically.
  3. No state across gexit. x registers are dead after gexit. Millicode state that must persist lives in CSRs or hidden memory.
  4. Interrupts only at guest boundaries. Millicode runs to completion.

docs.title: Entry and exit
docs.text:
The hardware decoder enters millicode with the opword, up to four extension words and the next sequential PC already in registers (see Millicode entry points). At entry gpc holds the instruction's own address; millicode writes the next PC to gpc and executes gexit, which retires the guest instruction, checks interrupts and trace, and resumes the guest stream.

gfault/gfaultr raise a guest exception: control transfers to the exception entry point, which is itself millicode and builds the 68k stack frame.

docs.title: Floating point
docs.text:
The FP extension (major 48, FP) gives the core's double-precision FPU to millicode. FP registers are a namespace of their own: f0-f7 hold the guest's FP0-FP7 as IEEE doubles, f8-f15 are millicode temporaries. An FP op names them in the same 6-bit register fields; the spec lists which fields of an op are FP (fp: [rd, rs1, rs2]), and the decoder carries that as fpregs. The ops:

  • fadd.d fsub.d fmul.d fdiv.d fsqrt.d, fmul.s fdiv.s (singles in bits 31:0), fcvt.s.d fcvt.d.s: IEEE 754 under the FPCR's rounding mode (CSR fpcr bits 5:4, the 68k's order), denormals in full, tininess before rounding with UF for every tiny result (exact or not: the 68881's UNFL), and the 68881's NaN rules (rs1's NaN, else rs2's, quieted; the default NaN all ones, 0x7fffffffffffffff). Each ORs the IEEE exceptions it raises into CSR fflags (NV DZ OF UF NX); a read of fflags sees every older FP op's.
  • fmov.d fneg.d fabs.d: bit copies, no exceptions.
  • fsethi fsetlo (an x register into half of an FP register, the other half kept) and fgethi fgetlo (half of an FP register into an x register): the only paths between the files. Memory never holds FP registers directly: millicode loads and stores them as integers, so misaligned, uncached and faulting operands take the integer paths' mechanisms.

These are the semantics of q800sim's FPU (Berkeley SoftFloat-3 binary64 with the 68881's NaN and underflow rules), which is the reference: the 68881's 80-bit values exist only in memory, converted by millicode at FMOVE.X / FMOVEM.X (millicode/fpd_num.h, q800sim's to_d / from_d exactly). millicode/fpd.c implements FPU-gen, FScc / FDBcc / FTRAPcc, FBcc, FSAVE and FRESTORE on them (see its header): NaN operands are handled in software before any FP op runs, as q800sim does before calling SoftFloat. The transcendentals, FMOD / FREM and packed decimal are not there yet (brk 30 / brk 31). Extended precision is double everywhere: every load of an extended value is rounded to a double (FMOVE.X to nearest, FMOVEM.X with the FPCR's rounding mode, as q800sim). CSRs fpcr fpsr fpiar are the 68881's registers; fpused is the FSAVE frame state (null until the FPU is used).

The model (model/uisa_machine.cc fpop) computes the FP ops with the host's arithmetic and fenv, the NaN rules applied explicitly; its flags are an AArch64 host's (tininess before rounding), plus UF for an exact subnormal result. uisa_m68k_state carries the FPU when fp_valid says so; without it the engine and the shadow leave coprocessor-1 instructions to the host.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Hidden memory base and size, and whether hot handlers live in on-chip RAM.
  • Whether the 68040 table walk is hardware (from the rv64core/superdupersparc walker) or a millicode TLB refill using probe and a TLB-write operation not yet defined here.
  • The FP extension's next step (majors 49-52 stay reserved): the transcendentals and FMOD / FREM in millicode, with q800sim calling the same C code. Extended precision stays double (decided 2026-11-20: no floatx80 soft-float). The double-precision ops are in (Floating point).
  • Exact N and V results of the BCD ops, which the 68040 leaves undefined; match the reference model (Previous) once co-simulation runs.
  • Whether 16-bit displacements in the PLA's uops need a matching millicode encoding (the M format has a 12-bit displacement).

No flags, full 32-bit results, unless the row says otherwise. Operand names: a = rs1, b = rs2 or the decoded immediate.

Mnemonic Format Encoding Operands Semantics Notes add R ALU fn=0 rd, rs1, rs2 r = a + b; sub R ALU fn=1 rd, rs1, rs2 r = a - b; and R ALU fn=2 rd, rs1, rs2 r = a & b; or R ALU fn=3 rd, rs1, rs2 r = a | b; xor R ALU fn=4 rd, rs1, rs2 r = a ^ b; andn R ALU fn=5 rd, rs1, rs2 r = a & ~b; orn R ALU fn=6 rd, rs1, rs2 r = a | ~b; sll R ALU fn=7 rd, rs1, rs2 r = a << (b & 31); srl R ALU fn=8 rd, rs1, rs2 r = a >> (b & 31); sra R ALU fn=9 rd, rs1, rs2 r = (uint32_t)((int32_t)a >> (b & 31)); rol R ALU fn=10 rd, rs1, rs2 r = ROL32(a, b & 31); ror R ALU fn=11 rd, rs1, rs2 r = ROL32(a, (32 - (b & 31)) & 31); slt R ALU fn=12 rd, rs1, rs2 r = (int32_t)a < (int32_t)b; sltu R ALU fn=13 rd, rs1, rs2 r = a < b; min R ALU fn=14 rd, rs1, rs2 r = (int32_t)a < (int32_t)b ? a : b; max R ALU fn=15 rd, rs1, rs2 r = (int32_t)a > (int32_t)b ? a : b; minu R ALU fn=16 rd, rs1, rs2 r = a < b ? a : b; maxu R ALU fn=17 rd, rs1, rs2 r = a > b ? a : b; mul R ALU fn=18 rd, rs1, rs2 r = a * b; mulh R ALU fn=19 rd, rs1, rs2 r = (uint32_t)(((int64_t)(int32_t)a * (int64_t)(int32_t)b) >> 32); mulhu R ALU fn=20 rd, rs1, rs2 r = (uint32_t)(((uint64_t)a * (uint64_t)b) >> 32); div R ALU fn=21 rd, rs1, rs2 r = (b == 0) ? 0xffffffffu : ((a == 0x80000000u && b == 0xffffffffu) ? a : (uint32_t)((int32_t)a / (int32_t)b)); Never faults. Division by zero returns all ones. divu R ALU fn=22 rd, rs1, rs2 r = (b == 0) ? 0xffffffffu : a / b; Never faults. rem R ALU fn=23 rd, rs1, rs2 r = (b == 0) ? a : ((a == 0x80000000u && b == 0xffffffffu) ? 0 : (uint32_t)((int32_t)a % (int32_t)b)); remu R ALU fn=24 rd, rs1, rs2 r = (b == 0) ? a : a % b; clz R ALU fn=25 rd, rs1 r = a ? __builtin_clz(a) : 32; ctz R ALU fn=26 rd, rs1 r = a ? __builtin_ctz(a) : 32; cpop R ALU fn=27 rd, rs1 r = __builtin_popcount(a); rev8 R ALU fn=28 rd, rs1 r = __builtin_bswap32(a); sext8 R ALU fn=29 rd, rs1 r = (uint32_t)SX(a, 8); sext16 R ALU fn=30 rd, rs1 r = (uint32_t)SX(a, 16); zext8 R ALU fn=31 rd, rs1 r = a & 0xffu; zext16 R ALU fn=32 rd, rs1 r = a & 0xffffu; czeqz R ALU fn=33 rd, rs1, rs2 r = (b == 0) ? 0 : a; Conditional zero (branch-free select building block). cznez R ALU fn=34 rd, rs1, rs2 r = (b != 0) ? 0 : a; mrg8 R ALU fn=35 rd, rs1, rs2 r = (a & ~0xffu) | (b & 0xffu); Explicit byte merge: upper 24 bits from rs1, low byte from rs2. mrg16 R ALU fn=36 rd, rs1, rs2 r = (a & ~0xffffu) | (b & 0xffffu); rdccr R ALU fn=37 rd r = CCR_PACK(xin, nin, zin, vin, cin); Copy the renamed flags into a register (CCR layout). (reads nzvc+x) wrccr R ALU fn=38 rs1 CCR_UNPACK(a, X, N, Z, V, C); Load the renamed flags from a register (CCR layout). (writes nzvc+x) rdg R ALU fn=39 rd, rs1 r = GREG_READ(a & 31); Read guest register g[rs1 & 31] (namespace index 32 + n): D0-D7, A0-A7, gpc, gsr are 0-17. An index of 18-31 is a millicode fault (registers 50-63 are not reachable). Index is data, so rename serializes. (serializes) wrg R ALU fn=40 rs1, rs2 GREG_WRITE(a & 31, b); Write rs2 to guest register g[rs1 & 31], 0-17 as rdg; an index of 18-31 is a millicode fault and writes nothing. Serializes. (serializes) sh1add R ALU fn=42 rd, rs1, rs2 r = a + (b << 1); Scaled-index add (68k (d8,An,Xn*2)). sh2add R ALU fn=43 rd, rs1, rs2 r = a + (b << 2); sh3add R ALU fn=44 rd, rs1, rs2 r = a + (b << 3); bfmask R ALU fn=41 rd, rs2 r = BF_MASK(b); Mask of the 68k bitfield described by rs2 (offset in bits 4:0 from the MSB, width in bits 9:5, 0 means 32), wrapping like a register bitfield. sel.<cc> R ALU fn=0x40+cc rd, rs1, rs2 r = COND ? a : b; rd = cond ? rs1 : rs2, on the guest condition. cc: t f hi ls cc cs ne eq vc vs pl mi ge lt gt le. (reads nzvc) s.<cc> R ALU fn=0x50+cc rd r = COND ? 0xffffffffu : 0; rd = cond ? all ones : 0 (Scc building block; follow with mov.8 to merge). cc: t f hi ls cc cs ne eq vc vs pl mi ge lt gt le. (reads nzvc) addi I ADDI rd, rs1, imm r = a + b; andi I ANDI rd, rs1, imm r = a & b; Immediate is zero-extended. ori I ORI rd, rs1, imm r = a | b; Immediate is zero-extended. xori I XORI rd, rs1, imm r = a ^ b; Immediate is zero-extended. slti I SLTI rd, rs1, imm r = (int32_t)a < (int32_t)b; sltiu I SLTIU rd, rs1, imm r = a < b; slli I SLLI rd, rs1, imm r = a << (b & 31); srli I SRLI rd, rs1, imm r = a >> (b & 31); srai I SRAI rd, rs1, imm r = (uint32_t)((int32_t)a >> (b & 31)); rori I RORI rd, rs1, imm r = ROL32(a, (32 - (b & 31)) & 31); lui U LUI rd, imm r = b << 12; auipc U AUIPC rd, imm r = pc + (b << 12); jal J JAL rd, imm r = pc + 4; npc = pc + b; jalr I JALR rd, rs1, imm r = pc + 4; npc = (a + b) & ~3u; call L CALL imm CSTACK_PUSH(pc + 4); npc = pc + b; Push the return address on the hardware millicode return stack. Overflow is a millicode fault. b.<cc> B BR cond=cc rs1, rs2, imm if (COND) npc = pc + IMM; Compare two registers and branch. Millicode control flow; never reads guest flags. cc: eq ne lt ge ltu geu. b.u B BR cond=6 imm if (uin) npc = pc + IMM; Branch if the millicode predicate u is set. Encoded in the BR major with cond 6; the rs1 and rs2 fields are zero (the assembler writes zeros; the decoder ignores them). The register compare branches never read u. (reads u) b.nu B BR cond=7 imm if (!uin) npc = pc + IMM; Branch if the millicode predicate u is clear (a probe failed): BR with cond 7, rs1 = rs2 = 0 as b.u. (reads u) bcc.<cc> C BCC cond=cc imm if (COND) npc = pc + b; Branch on a guest condition. cc: t f hi ls cc cs ne eq vc vs pl mi ge lt gt le. (reads nzvc) bfextu R BF fn=0 rd, rs1, rs2 r = BF_EXTU(a, b); Extract the field described by rs2 (offset 4:0, width 9:5), zero-extended. bfexts R BF fn=1 rd, rs1, rs2 r = BF_EXTS(a, b); bfffo R BF fn=2 rd, rs1, rs2 r = BF_FFO(a, b); Offset of the first 1 bit in the field, or offset+width if none (68k BFFFO). bfextui BFI BFI fn=0 rd, rs1, off, wid r = BF_EXTU(a, b); bfextsi BFI BFI fn=1 rd, rs1, off, wid r = BF_EXTS(a, b); bfinsi BFI BFI fn=2 rd, rs1, off, wid r = BF_INS(OLD, a, b); Insert the low wid bits of rs1 into the field of rd. rd is also a source (old value), so the op reads rd and rs1. bx BFI BFI fn=3 rs1, off, wid npc = pc + 4 + (((a >> BF_OFF(b)) & MSK(BF_WID(b))) << 2); Indexed branch (n-way dispatch): take the wid-bit field of rs1 starting at bit off (counted from the LSB here, 1 <= wid <= 15) as an index into a table of one-instruction slots that follows the bx, usually jal to each case. Predicted like an indirect jump. gexit S SYS fn=0 End of the guest instruction: retire it, take pending interrupts/trace, resume the guest stream at gpc. gfault S SYS fn=1 imm Raise guest exception vector imm8. Transfers to the exception entry point. gfaultr S SYS fn=16 rs1 Raise the guest exception whose vector is in rs1 (TRAP #n, computed vectors). gbcc.<cc> CG GBCC cond=cc imm if (COND) GNPC_SET(GPC_INSN + b); Guest conditional branch (Bcc, BRA via gbcc.t). cc: t f hi ls cc cs ne eq vc vs pl mi ge lt gt le. (reads nzvc) gbz BG GBZ cond=0 rs1, imm if (a == 0) GNPC_SET(GPC_INSN + b); Guest branch if rs1 is zero. gbnz BG GBZ cond=1 rs1, imm if (a != 0) GNPC_SET(GPC_INSN + b); Guest branch if rs1 is nonzero (DBF). gjr I GJR rs1, imm GNPC_SET(a + b); Guest jump to rs1 + imm (JMP, JSR, RTS). gjr x0, abs jumps to an absolute address. gpushr I GPUSHR rd, imm GSTORE(GDATA, a - 4, 4, GPC_INSN + b); r = a - 4; Push a return address: mem[rd - 4] = guest instruction address + imm (its length); rd = rd - 4. One register source and one result (rd is tied to rs1); the data is an immediate. A speculative store whose register result is ready at address generation. gpcaddi I GPCADDI rd, imm r = GPC_INSN + b; rd = guest instruction address + imm (return addresses, PC-relative operands). ret S SYS fn=2 npc = CSTACK_POP(); Return through the hardware millicode return stack. Underflow is a millicode fault. csrr S SYS fn=3 rd, csr r = CSR_READ(IMM); csrw S SYS fn=4 csr, rs1 CSR_WRITE(IMM, a & CSR_WMASK[IMM & 0xff]); (serializes) csrs S SYS fn=5 csr, rs1 CSR_WRITE(IMM, (CSR_READ(IMM) | a) & CSR_WMASK[IMM & 0xff]); (serializes) csrc S SYS fn=6 csr, rs1 CSR_WRITE(IMM, CSR_READ(IMM) & ~a & CSR_WMASK[IMM & 0xff]); (serializes) unlock S SYS fn=7 /* ends the locked sequence; no functional effect */ End a locked sequence without a store (failed CAS compare). (serializes) fence S SYS fn=8 Order all earlier memory accesses before all later ones. (serializes) tlbflush S SYS fn=9 rs1, imm MMU_FLUSH(a, IMM); Guest TLB flush. imm bit0: page (address in rs1) vs all; bit1: non-global entries only; bit2: user-only (FC). Covers PFLUSH/PFLUSHN/PFLUSHA. (serializes) cpush S SYS fn=10 rs1, imm CACHE_OP(a, IMM, 1); Write back and invalidate guest cache lines. imm bits1:0 cache (1=D, 2=I, 3=both); bits3:2 scope (0=line, 1=page, 2=all). Address in rs1. (serializes) cinv S SYS fn=11 rs1, imm CACHE_OP(a, IMM, 0); Invalidate without write back. Same imm encoding as cpush. (serializes) irqack S SYS fn=12 rd, rs1 Acknowledge the interrupt at level rs1; rd = vector (autovector if none supplied). (serializes) stop S SYS fn=13 Wait for an interrupt (68k STOP, after millicode has loaded SR). (serializes) halt S SYS fn=14 imm Stop the machine (simulation / debug). imm is a status code. (serializes) brk S SYS fn=15 imm Debug breakpoint. (serializes) fadd.d R FP fn=0 f:rd, f:rs1, f:rs2 fd = fs1 + fs2 (binary64). fsub.d R FP fn=1 f:rd, f:rs1, f:rs2 fd = fs1 - fs2. fmul.d R FP fn=2 f:rd, f:rs1, f:rs2 fd = fs1 * fs2. fdiv.d R FP fn=3 f:rd, f:rs1, f:rs2 fd = fs1 / fs2 (the shared iterative divider). fsqrt.d R FP fn=4 f:rd, f:rs1 fd = sqrt(fs1) (the shared iterative divider). fmul.s R FP fn=5 f:rd, f:rs1, f:rs2 fd = fs1 * fs2 (binary32, operands and result in bits 31:0). fdiv.s R FP fn=6 f:rd, f:rs1, f:rs2 fd = fs1 / fs2 (binary32). fcvt.s.d R FP fn=7 f:rd, f:rs1 fd = fs1 rounded to binary32 (overflow, underflow, inexact; a NaN keeps its sign and payload top, quieted). fcvt.d.s R FP fn=8 f:rd, f:rs1 fd = the binary32 in fs1 widened to binary64 (exact; a signaling NaN is quieted and raises invalid). fmov.d R FP fn=9 f:rd, f:rs1 fd = fs1, all 64 bits. No exceptions. fneg.d R FP fn=10 f:rd, f:rs1 fd = fs1 with bit 63 inverted (NaNs too). No exceptions. fabs.d R FP fn=11 f:rd, f:rs1 fd = fs1 with bit 63 cleared (NaNs too). No exceptions. fsethi R FP fn=16 f:rd, rs1 fd[63:32] = rs1; fd[31:0] keeps its value (fd is a source). An integer-to-FP move. fsetlo R FP fn=17 f:rd, rs1 fd[31:0] = rs1; fd[63:32] keeps its value (fd is a source). fgethi R FP fn=18 rd, f:rs1 rd = fs1[63:32]. An FP-to-integer move. fgetlo R FP fn=19 rd, f:rs1 rd = fs1[31:0].

docs.title: Guest-semantic operations
docs.text:
Each family expands into sized forms (see Sized operations above). <f>.8/<f>.16 merge into rd and are two-address (rs1 = rd); <f>.32 is three-address; <f>.8z/<f>.16z zero-fill and do not read the old rd. Families marked imm also have <f>i.<sz>[z] forms with a 6-bit unsigned immediate. Every form has a .nf variant that writes no flags.

Family fn Kind Sizes imm Reads Writes Notes add 0 binary 8,16,32 yes - N Z V C X addx 1 binary 8,16,32 X Z N Z V C X Z is sticky: cleared if the result is nonzero, otherwise unchanged. sub 2 binary 8,16,32 yes - N Z V C X subx 3 binary 8,16,32 X Z N Z V C X neg 4 unary 8,16,32 - N Z V C X negx 5 unary 8,16,32 X Z N Z V C X cmp 6 compare 8,16,32 yes - N Z V C Flags of rs1 - rs2. X unaffected. and 7 binary 8,16,32 yes - N Z V C or 8 binary 8,16,32 yes - N Z V C eor 9 binary 8,16,32 yes - N Z V C not 10 unary 8,16,32 - N Z V C mov 11 unary 8,16,32 yes - N Z V C MOVE / TST. mov.8z x0, rs gives TST.B. lsl 12 binary 8,16,32 yes X N Z V C X Count is rs2 mod 64. A zero count clears C and leaves X; X is therefore always read. lsr 13 binary 8,16,32 yes X N Z V C X asl 14 binary 8,16,32 yes X N Z V C X V is set if the most significant bit changes at any time during the shift. asr 15 binary 8,16,32 yes X N Z V C X rol 16 binary 8,16,32 yes - N Z V C X unaffected. ror 17 binary 8,16,32 yes - N Z V C roxl 18 binary 8,16,32 yes X N Z V C X Rotate through X (n+1 bits). A zero count sets C to X. roxr 19 binary 8,16,32 yes X N Z V C X abcd 20 binary 8 X Z N Z V C X Packed BCD add with X. N and V are undefined on the 68040; the values here are placeholders to be matched to the reference model. sbcd 21 binary 8 X Z N Z V C X Packed BCD rs1 - rs2 - X. N and V undefined (placeholders). nbcd 22 unary 8 X Z N Z V C X mulu 23 full 16,32 - N Z V C .16: 16x16->32 (MULU.W). .32: low 32 bits, V on overflow (MULU.L 32-bit result). High half: base mulhu. muls 24 full 16,32 - N Z V C divu 25 tiedfull 16,32 N Z V N Z V C .16: 32/16 -> remainder:quotient (DIVU.W); on overflow rd, N and Z are unchanged, V is set and C cleared (as the 68040 does). .32: quotient only; remainder via base remu. Trap: zero divisor: rd, N, Z and V unchanged, C cleared, and the zero-divide trap (vector 5) taken once the instruction retires divs 26 tiedfull 16,32 N Z V N Z V C Trap: zero divisor: as divu ext 27 unary 16,32 - N Z V C .16: EXT.W (byte to word, merged). .32: EXT.L (word to long). extb 28 unary 32 - N Z V C EXTB.L (byte to long). btst 29 compare 8,32 yes N V C N Z V C Bit test: only Z changes, so NZVC is read and merged. .8 for memory operands (bit mod 8), .32 for Dn (bit mod 32). bchg 30 binary 8,32 yes N V C N Z V C bclr 31 binary 8,32 yes N V C N Z V C bset 32 binary 8,32 yes N V C N Z V C

docs.title: Guest-op semantics
docs.text:
C reference semantics, exactly as compiled into the generated ISS header. n = operand width, m = MSK(n), xin..cin = incoming flags. Setting T to a vector flags a trap: the uop's instruction retires (its other results, such as an address-register update, stand) and the exception is then taken with the next PC stacked, as the 68k does for a zero divide.

add

uint64_t s = (uint64_t)(a & m) + (b & m);
r = (uint32_t)s & m;
C = (s >> n) & 1; X = C;
V = MSB((a ^ r) & (b ^ r), n);
N = MSB(r, n); Z = (r == 0);

addx

uint64_t s = (uint64_t)(a & m) + (b & m) + xin;
r = (uint32_t)s & m;
C = (s >> n) & 1; X = C;
V = MSB((a ^ r) & (b ^ r), n);
N = MSB(r, n); Z = zin && (r == 0);

sub

r = (a - b) & m;
C = (b & m) > (a & m); X = C;
V = MSB((a ^ b) & (a ^ r), n);
N = MSB(r, n); Z = (r == 0);

subx

r = (a - b - xin) & m;
C = (uint64_t)(b & m) + xin > (a & m); X = C;
V = MSB((a ^ b) & (a ^ r), n);
N = MSB(r, n); Z = zin && (r == 0);

neg

r = (0u - b) & m;
C = (b & m) != 0; X = C;
V = MSB(b & r, n);
N = MSB(r, n); Z = (r == 0);

negx

r = (0u - b - xin) & m;
C = ((uint64_t)(b & m) + xin) != 0; X = C;
V = MSB(b & r, n);
N = MSB(r, n); Z = zin && (r == 0);

cmp

r = (a - b) & m;
C = (b & m) > (a & m);
V = MSB((a ^ b) & (a ^ r), n);
N = MSB(r, n); Z = (r == 0);

and

r = (a & b) & m; N = MSB(r, n); Z = (r == 0); V = 0; C = 0;

or

r = (a | b) & m; N = MSB(r, n); Z = (r == 0); V = 0; C = 0;

eor

r = (a ^ b) & m; N = MSB(r, n); Z = (r == 0); V = 0; C = 0;

not

r = ~b & m; N = MSB(r, n); Z = (r == 0); V = 0; C = 0;

mov

r = b & m; N = MSB(r, n); Z = (r == 0); V = 0; C = 0;

lsl

unsigned k = b & 63; uint64_t v = a & m;
if (k == 0) { r = (uint32_t)v; C = 0; X = xin; }
else { C = (k <= n) ? ((v >> (n - k)) & 1) : 0; X = C; r = (k < n) ? (uint32_t)((v << k) & m) : 0; }
V = 0; N = MSB(r, n); Z = (r == 0);

lsr

unsigned k = b & 63; uint64_t v = a & m;
if (k == 0) { r = (uint32_t)v; C = 0; X = xin; }
else { C = (k <= n) ? ((v >> (k - 1)) & 1) : 0; X = C; r = (k < n) ? (uint32_t)(v >> k) : 0; }
V = 0; N = MSB(r, n); Z = (r == 0);

asl

unsigned k = b & 63; uint64_t v = a & m;
if (k == 0) { r = (uint32_t)v; C = 0; X = xin; V = 0; }
else {
  C = (k <= n) ? ((v >> (n - k)) & 1) : 0; X = C;
  r = (k < n) ? (uint32_t)((v << k) & m) : 0;
  if (k >= n) V = (v != 0);
  else { uint64_t hm = MSK(k + 1) << (n - 1 - k); uint64_t t = v & hm; V = !(t == 0 || t == hm); }
}
N = MSB(r, n); Z = (r == 0);

asr

unsigned k = b & 63; int64_t sv = SX(a, n);
if (k == 0) { r = a & m; C = 0; X = xin; }
else { C = (k <= n) ? ((sv >> (k - 1)) & 1) : MSB(a, n); X = C; r = (uint32_t)(sv >> (k < 63 ? k : 63)) & m; }
V = 0; N = MSB(r, n); Z = (r == 0);

rol

unsigned k = b & 63; uint64_t v = a & m;
if (k == 0) { r = (uint32_t)v; C = 0; }
else { unsigned s = k % n; r = (uint32_t)(s ? (((v << s) | (v >> (n - s))) & m) : v); C = r & 1; }
V = 0; N = MSB(r, n); Z = (r == 0);

ror

unsigned k = b & 63; uint64_t v = a & m;
if (k == 0) { r = (uint32_t)v; C = 0; }
else { unsigned s = k % n; r = (uint32_t)(s ? (((v >> s) | (v << (n - s))) & m) : v); C = MSB(r, n); }
V = 0; N = MSB(r, n); Z = (r == 0);

roxl

unsigned k = (b & 63) % (n + 1); uint64_t w = ((uint64_t)xin << n) | (a & m); uint64_t wm = (1ull << (n + 1)) - 1;   /* n + 1 bits: MSK() saturates at 32 */
if (k) w = ((w << k) | (w >> (n + 1 - k))) & wm;
r = (uint32_t)(w & m); X = (w >> n) & 1; C = X;
V = 0; N = MSB(r, n); Z = (r == 0);

roxr

unsigned k = (b & 63) % (n + 1); uint64_t w = ((uint64_t)xin << n) | (a & m); uint64_t wm = (1ull << (n + 1)) - 1;   /* n + 1 bits: MSK() saturates at 32 */
if (k) w = ((w >> k) | (w << (n + 1 - k))) & wm;
r = (uint32_t)(w & m); X = (w >> n) & 1; C = X;
V = 0; N = MSB(r, n); Z = (r == 0);

abcd

int lo = (a & 15) + (b & 15) + xin;
if (lo > 9) lo += 6;
int s = lo + (a & 0xf0) + (b & 0xf0);
C = s > 0x99; X = C;
if (C) s -= 0xa0;
r = (uint32_t)s & 0xff;
Z = zin && (r == 0); N = MSB(r, 8); V = 0;

sbcd

int lo = (int)(a & 15) - (int)(b & 15) - (int)xin;
int s = (int)(a & 0xf0) - (int)(b & 0xf0) + lo;
if (lo < 0) s -= 6;
C = s < 0; X = C;
if (C) s += 0xa0;
r = (uint32_t)s & 0xff;
Z = zin && (r == 0); N = MSB(r, 8); V = 0;

nbcd

int lo = 0 - (int)(b & 15) - (int)xin;
int s = 0 - (int)(b & 0xf0) + lo;
if (lo < 0) s -= 6;
C = s < 0; X = C;
if (C) s += 0xa0;
r = (uint32_t)s & 0xff;
Z = zin && (r == 0); N = MSB(r, 8); V = 0;

mulu

if (n == 16) { r = (a & 0xffff) * (b & 0xffff); V = 0; }
else { uint64_t p = (uint64_t)a * b; r = (uint32_t)p; V = (p >> 32) != 0; }
N = MSB(r, 32); Z = (r == 0); C = 0;

muls

if (n == 16) { r = (uint32_t)(SX(a, 16) * SX(b, 16)); V = 0; }
else { int64_t p = (int64_t)(int32_t)a * (int32_t)b; r = (uint32_t)p; V = p != (int64_t)(int32_t)r; }
N = MSB(r, 32); Z = (r == 0); C = 0;

divu

if ((n == 16 ? (b & 0xffff) : b) == 0) { r = a; T = 5; }
else if (n == 16) {
  uint32_t d = b & 0xffff, q = a / d, rm = a % d;
  if (q > 0xffff) { r = a; V = 1; }
  else { r = (rm << 16) | q; V = 0; N = MSB(q, 16); Z = (q == 0); }
} else { r = a / b; V = 0; N = MSB(r, 32); Z = (r == 0); }
C = 0;

divs

if ((n == 16 ? (b & 0xffff) : b) == 0) { r = a; T = 5; }
else if (n == 16) {

docs.title: Millicode entry points
docs.text:
insn: Guest instruction not handled by the PLA. Target = dispatch_base[opword].

  • x1: opword (zero-extended)
  • x2: extension words 0:1 (word 0 in bits 31:16)
  • x3: extension words 2:3
  • x4: address of the next sequential guest instruction

exception: Guest exception raised by a guest access fault, gfault, or a decode-time condition (illegal, privilege, line A/F).

  • x1: vector number (2 for an access fault)
  • x2: guest PC to stack (gpc when raised; the faulting instruction for access faults)
  • x3: address of the instruction that raised it (format 2 frames)

Access faults (vector 2) leave the 68040 frame fields in the fault_* and wb* CSRs.

interrupt: Taken at a guest instruction boundary when the pending level exceeds the SR mask.

  • x1: interrupt level
  • x2: vector number (from the interrupt acknowledge; 24 + level when autovectored)

trace: Taken after gexit when trace is pending.

  • x1: address of the traced instruction

reset: Power-on and RESET. All registers undefined.

mfault: Internal millicode error (misaligned hidden access, return-stack overflow/underflow, illegal micro-instruction). Halts for debug.

  • x1: cause
  • x2: millicode PC

docs.title: SoftFloat in millicode
docs.text:
softfloat.h is the floatx80 (68881/68040 extended precision) arithmetic the FPU millicode will be built from, written in the millicode C subset (compiler/README.md). It is a port of the SoftFloat that Previous uses (previous/src/softfloat: QEMU's SoftFloat 2a with WinUAE's SOFTFLOAT_68K changes), configured as Previous configures it for a 68040, so co-simulation against Previous can compare FP results and exception flags bit for bit.

The port keeps the original's structure, names, constants and gotos; pointer out-parameters became references and float_status * became float_status &. Every function is inline: SoftFloat nests helpers deeper than the 4-entry millicode return stack, and inlining also lets register allocation see each operation whole.

docs.title: The instruction handler (millicode/fpu.c)
docs.text:
fpu.c is the FPU-gen handler (opwords F200-F23F) built on this port. It follows Previous's fpuop_arithmetic step for step and is tested against it: tests/fpu links Previous's own cpu/fpp.c (with stubbed CPU and memory hooks) and runs random instructions and machine states through both, comparing data and address registers, FP registers, FPCR, FPSR, FPIAR, the next PC and the exception taken. make runs 20,000 cases (about 2 s); 300,000 pass, of which 146,000 complete normally and are compared bit for bit.

Done: opclass 000/010 (FPm or <ea> to FPn) for the 68040's hardware set, every source format but packed, every addressing mode with a brief index word; FMOVE FPcr to/from Dn/An; the F-line and illegal traps for opmodes with no instruction; FPSR condition codes, exception and accrued bytes.

State: FP0-FP7 in scratch memory (CSR_SCRATCH_BASE + 12n, FMOVEM extended layout), FPCR/FPSR/FPIAR in their CSRs.

fpu.c is not in dispatch.yaml yet: the shadow model has no FP state and rejects hidden-memory accesses, so routing FPU-gen to it now would turn instructions that pass into failures. Hooking it up needs FP registers and FPCR/FPSR/FPIAR in the shadow state (and Previous's hook to fill them), hidden-memory support in the model, and program-space (.gp) loads looked up in the IFETCH log.

docs.title: What the 68040 traps (and the millicode will too)
docs.text:
The millicode implements exactly the 68040's hardware FP set and traps the rest to the OS's FPSP, as the real chip does and as Previous does (fpu_no_unimplemented, cpu/fpp.c):

  • Unimplemented instructions (fault_if_unimplemented_680x0): every FPU-gen opmode except FMOVE, FSQRT, FABS, FNEG, FADD, FSUB, FMUL, FDIV, FSGLMUL, FSGLDIV, FCMP, FTST and their FS/FD rounding variants. That covers the transcendentals, FINT/FINTRZ, FGETEXP/FGETMAN, FSCALE, FMOD/FREM and FMOVECR, so none of them is ported here.
  • Unimplemented data types (normalize_or_fault_if_no_denormal_support, fault_if_no_packed_support): a denormal or unnormal source or destination operand, except an unnormal zero (which becomes a zero), and any packed-decimal operand. The arithmetic above therefore only ever sees normalized numbers, zeros, infinities and NaNs.

docs.title: ucc: the uisa millicode compiler
docs.text:
ucc compiles a small subset of C to uisa millicode assembly that tools/uisa.py assembles. It exists because millicode that is too large to write by hand (SoftFloat-style extended-precision FP first) still has to obey the millicode rules: no memory stack, no spilling, a 4-deep hardware return stack, and register allocation across the whole program.

A flex/bison front end builds an AST whose nodes emit three-address code straight into basic blocks. The middle end builds SSA (Lengauer-Tarjan dominators, dominance frontiers, liveness-pruned phi placement, renaming along the dominator tree) and optimizes it. The back end selects uisa instructions, allocates registers for the whole program at once while the code is still in SSA, and only then takes it out of SSA with parallel copies.

make compiler                       # CMake build into build/compiler (needs flex, bison 3, z3, python3 + PyYAML)
build/compiler/ucc [-o out.s] [-v] [--dump-tac] [-O0|-O2] [--rlimit n] file.c
python3 compiler/tests/test_ucc.py [iterations [name]]  # compiler tests (also run by `make`)

z3 is found under /opt/local (MacPorts: sudo port install z3), /opt/homebrew or /usr/local. -v prints the size of the allocation problem, the move cost z3 reached, the greedy allocation's cost and the z3 resource units used.

Millicode written in C lives in millicode/*.c. When a .c file is listed in millicode/dispatch.yaml, tools/gen_millicode.py compiles it to build/millicode/<name>.s and assembles it with the hand-written sources. Labels must be unique across all sources (checked). millicode/bitfield.c (BFTST/BFEXTU/BFEXTS/BFFFO) is the first routine built this way.

docs.title: Language
docs.text:
• Types: u8 u16 u32 u64 s8 s16 s32 s64, plus int (= s32), unsigned (= u32) and void. Every value is kept canonical for its type (u8 zero-extended, s8 sign-extended, ...), so promotion costs nothing.
  • Integer constants follow C with s32 u32 s64 u64 in place of int unsigned long long unsigned long long: the first type that holds the value (unsigned only for hex/octal or with a u suffix); ll/ull force 64 bits.
  • C's integer promotions and usual arithmetic conversions; casts. >> is arithmetic on signed and logical on unsigned (promoted) operands; / % divide signed or unsigned the same way. s64 holds every u32, so s64 op u32 is s64, as in C.
  • Operators: + - * / % & | ^ ~ << >> ! && || ?:, comparisons, = and the compound assignments, prefix and postfix ++ --.
  • Statements: blocks, declarations anywhere (with initializers), if/else, while, do/while, for (with a declaration), switch with fallthrough (case labels directly inside the switch body), break, continue, return.
  • Functions with parameters and a return value; global and local const integer declarations (constant expressions). Functions may be called before their definition.
  • struct name { fields }; with scalar or struct fields, value semantics (copy, assign, pass, return; .field access and assignment), and typedef type name;. After its definition a struct's name is a type name, as in C++.
  • inline functions are expanded at every call: no call instruction, no return-stack depth, no register-allocation boundary. Only inline functions take reference parameters (u64 &z), which name the caller's variable, as SoftFloat's pointer out-parameters do, and only they return values wider than two words. Recursion through inline functions is an error.
  • Called (non-inline) functions take any number of argument words (a u64 is two, a struct its fields' words) and return at most two words.
  • #include "file" (relative to the including file; each file is read at most once; #pragma once is accepted and redundant). Diagnostics name the included file and its line.
  • entry void name(void) declares a millicode entry point: it is dispatched to (never called), may use the entry-ABI intrinsics, cannot return, and every path must end in a no-return intrinsic (__gexit, __gfault, ...).
  • extern T name(params) asm("ARGS -> RESULTS; reads R...; clobbers R...; depth N"); declares a hand-written routine in millicode/*.s and its register contract, so C millicode can call shared assembly helpers. ARGS and RESULTS name one x register per word (a two-word struct result comes back in two); reads lists entry-ABI registers (x1-x4) the routine reads, which the compiler passes implicitly and which keep their values up to the call (so only entry functions may call such a routine); clobbers lists the other registers it may write (x16-x19 ranges allowed); depth is the return-stack entries it uses, its own call included (default 1). The argument, result and clobbered registers are all treated as written by the call: nothing live across it is allocated to them, and a fixed register (an entry-ABI value) still needed after the call is an error. Example (millicode/bitfield.c): extern ea_res ea_addr(u32 ea, u32 size, u32 ext_off) asm("x20 x21 x22 -> x23 x4; reads x2 x3 x4; clobbers x16-x19 x24-x26; depth 3");
  • Not in the millicode language: pointers, arrays, unions, floats, globals that are not constants, the comma operator, char literals, string literals outside asm("..."), and the preprocessor beyond #include. Pointers, arrays, mutable globals and the comma operator exist in program mode (below) and are errors in millicode.

docs.title: 64-bit types
docs.text:
The front end splits every u64/s64 value into two 32-bit words (a variable becomes two source variables), so SSA, allocation and emission only ever see 32-bit values and each word is allocated, and dies, on its own.

operation lowering + - word add/sub, carry/borrow with sltu (4 instructions) * mul + mulhu + two cross muls; (u64)a * b with 32-bit operands is mul + mulhu << >> constant two or three word shifts << >> variable branch-free, 14 instructions; the count is taken mod 64 / % inline, no loop over bits (Hacker's Delight divdu/divlu): both high words 0 is one divu/remu; a 32-bit divisor is one divu for the high word plus a 64/32 step that estimates two 16-bit quotient digits with divu and corrects each at most twice; a wider divisor is normalized with clz, the same 64/32 step estimates the 32-bit quotient, and one multiply-subtract fixes it. Both paths share one copy of the 64/32 step; a divisor known to fit 32 bits (u64 / u32) emits only that path. About 110 instructions per division site, 25-60 executed. Signed divides the magnitudes. Unsigned powers of two become shifts and masks. Division by zero is undefined, as in C comparisons as branches: high words first, then the low words unsigned; as values: slt/sltu on the high words, combined calls a 64-bit argument takes two parameter registers (low word first); a 64-bit result comes back in two return registers, read by Call + CallRes and copied out as one parallel copy

Intrinsic arguments take the low word of a 64-bit value (C conversion to u32).

docs.title: Intrinsics
docs.text:
A switch with three or more cases becomes an n-way bx jump table (one jal slot per value) when its cases are small: switch ((x >> k) & (2^w - 1)) (k and the mask literals or named constants, w <= 15) indexes the table with that field of x directly, with no range check; any other 32-bit switch whose cases all lie in 0..63 checks the range (one branch to default) and then indexes. Other switches (negative or larger cases, 64-bit values, fewer cases) are compare chains.

(x >> k) & (2^w - 1) compiles to one bfextui (the assembler's extract rd, x, k, w), as does a mask too wide for andi.

compiler/gen_intrinsics.py generates the intrinsic table from spec/uisa.yaml through tools/uisa.py; nothing is hand-maintained. Every uisa instruction except millicode control flow (jal jalr call ret b.* bcc.*, which the compiler emits itself) and lui/auipc is available as __<mnemonic> with . replaced by _:

form example C signature base op clz rd, rs1 u32 __clz(u32) guest op, three-address / zfill add.32 rd, rs1, rs2 u32 __add_32(u32 a, u32 b) guest op, merge (rd tied to rs1) add.8 rd, rs2 u32 __add_8(u32 old, u32 b) guest compare (flags only) cmp.16 rs1, rs2 void __cmp_16(u32, u32) immediate forms addi.32 rd, rs1, imm6 u32 __addi_32(u32, const) load / probe ld.32.gd rd, d(rs1) u32 __ld_32_gd(u32 addr) store st.16.gd rd, d(rs1) void __st_16_gd(u32 addr, u32) store with base writeback st.32.pre.gd rs2, d(rs1) u32 __st_32_pre_gd(u32 base, u32 v, const d) system gfault imm, csrr rd, csr void __gfault(const), u32 __csrr(const)
  • Arguments that are immediates in the instruction must be constant expressions in range (checked against the spec's field widths and scales).
  • Address arguments: base + constant folds into the 12-bit displacement; constant addresses use x0 or lui.
  • Tied forms (merge, divu.16, bfinsi, writeback stores, gpushr) take the old destination value as their first argument; the allocator prefers to give the result the same register and otherwise inserts one move.
  • __rdg(i) / __wrg(i, v) with a constant i name the guest register directly (d3, gpc, ...) and the read feeds its uses directly when no write can intervene; with a run-time index they emit rdg/wrg.
  • Entry-ABI values (entry functions only): __opword() (x1), __ext01() (x2), __ext23() (x3), __next_pc() (x4), from the spec's insn entry point.
  • Predefined constants from the spec: D0..D7 A0..A7 GPC GSR (indices for __rdg/__wrg), CSR_<NAME> for every CSR, CCR_X CCR_N CCR_Z CCR_V CCR_C (bit masks in the rdccr/wrccr layout).
  • __gexit __gfault __gfaultr __halt __brk end control flow.
  • Flags are not modelled as values: intrinsics that read or write the renamed flags keep their program order, and the compiler never reorders anything.

docs.title: The idea: allocate in SSA, so "fits without spilling" is a static check
docs.text:
Millicode has no stack, so it cannot spill. The compiler therefore has to decide, before it allocates anything, whether every function fits in the 31 allocatable registers, and when one does not, say exactly where. For register allocation in general that question is graph colouring, which is NP-complete: the only way to know whether k registers suffice is to try. SSA form removes the difficulty:

  • The interference graph of an SSA program is chordal. In strict SSA every use is dominated by the value's single definition, so each live range is a connected subtree of the dominator tree, and the intersection graph of subtrees of a tree is chordal (Hack, Grund and Goos; Bouchez, Darte and Rastello; Brisk et al., all 2005-06).
  • For a chordal graph the chromatic number equals the largest clique, and colouring the vertices greedily in a perfect elimination order uses exactly that many colours. For SSA that order is simply the definitions in dominator-tree order.
  • The largest clique is the most values live at one program point. Subtrees of a tree that pairwise intersect share a common node (the Helly property), so a clique of live ranges is a set of values all live at the same point. MaxLive, the size of the largest live set, falls out of one liveness scan.

So a function needs exactly MaxLive registers, no more and no fewer. ucc computes it before allocation and rejects a function over 31 with the names of the values live at the peak, and when the check passes the greedy allocator (stage 1 below) is guaranteed to succeed; z3 only reduces moves. The rest of the design keeps that bound exact:

  • Leave SSA after allocation. Phis become parallel copies on the incoming edges, which only permute values already in registers: a cycle goes through a register free on that edge when there is one, otherwise three-xor swaps. Leaving SSA never needs an extra register.
  • Calls. Without a stack, a value live across a call must sit in a register that the callee, and everything it calls, never writes. A function's need is therefore MaxLive, or for some call the values live across it plus the callee's own need, whichever is larger; with recursion ruled out the call graph is acyclic, so this is computed callees first and checked against 31 too. There is no fixed calling convention: every function's parameter and result registers are part of the one whole-program solution.
  • Constraints that would break chordality are preferences. Copies, tied operands (merge forms), phi operands, call arguments and results only ask for the same register; when they cannot have it the emitter adds a move. The values pinned to registers (entry-ABI values in x1-x4) are all defined at function entry, the start of the elimination order.
  • Optimizations answer to the same bound. Value numbering and loop hoisting lengthen live ranges, so constants are shared only within a block and loop hoists are undone in any function they push over the budget.

Program mode (--program) has a stack and spills, so it uses a conventional Chaitin-Briggs allocator instead (below).

docs.title: Rules the compiler enforces
docs.text:
• No recursion. The call graph must be acyclic; a cycle is reported with its path.
  • Return-stack depth. Every chain of nested calls fits call_stack_depth (4) from the spec, counting the helper's own frame for helpers.
  • No spilling. Values live at once never exceed the 31 allocatable x registers (x1-x31). Over budget is a compile error that names the live values, before allocation; a second check adds up values live across each call and what the callee chain needs.
  • Whole-program allocation. One z3 problem covers every function. Hard constraints: interfering values differ; entry-ABI values stay in x1-x4; a value live across a call never sits in a register the callee or anything it calls writes. Soft constraints, weighted by loop depth: phi operands, copies, tied operands, call arguments and results, and return values share a register. Each function's parameter and return registers are part of the solution, so there is no fixed calling convention and no caller/callee-saved split. The result is verified independently of z3 before emission.
  • How the allocation is found. -O0 (the default, used by make and the tests) stops after stage 1: a valid allocation in a fraction of a second. -O2 is for deploy builds (make release compiles the millicode with it) and runs all three stages. Everything is deterministic (z3 runs under a resource budget, --rlimit, default 300M, never a wall-clock timeout, and the problem is keyed by value index, so the same source gives the same millicode on every machine):
  • Greedy. Functions callees first, values in dominance order (chordal coloring), each taking a register its colored preference partners use; then single values move where more partners are. Always feasible when the pressure checks pass; it is z3's starting point and the fallback.
  • Whole program (-O2). Up to 700 values, z3 gets a third of the budget to solve the whole problem and prove it optimal (t_u64div, 649 values: 30 s; t_u64div2, 570: 14 s; bitfield.c: well under a second).
  • Neighbourhoods (-O2). Otherwise, each step frees a small set of values, fixes every other one, and z3 solves that piece optimally as its own small problem (fixed neighbours become excluded registers, preferences to fixed values become one-register soft literals, call clobbers become exact exclusions). Loops go first, innermost first, each freeing the values of its own blocks (nested loops are already settled) and their interference neighbours, so the moves that execute most are optimal given their surroundings; then the values around the heaviest remaining moves, until nothing improves or the budget is spent.

-v reports the stage reached, how many loops were settled optimally and the remaining move cost per loop depth. On a SoftFloat-sized benchmark (compiler/tests/bench_alloc.c, 1674 values, four outer loops around inlined 64-bit divisions, inner correction loops) the weighted move cost goes from 1060 (greedy) to about 460 in 80 s, with every inner loop move removed; what remains is in the large outer loop bodies. - SSA optimization. Repeated to a fixed point: constant folding and algebraic simplification, copy propagation, dead-code removal, CFG cleanup, and global value numbering: a walk of the dominator tree with a scoped table of the values computed so far (ALU operations, extensions, frame addresses and the pure base intrinsics, with commutative operands ordered), so an expression that a dominating one already computed is reused instead of recomputed. Anything that reads state is never merged (guest registers, CSRs, guest flags, memory intrinsics); program-mode loads are reused within a block until the next store or call. After legalization a second pass merges the constants that legalization put in registers: within each block in millicode (a constant kept live across blocks would hold a register everywhere, and millicode cannot spill), across the dominator tree in program mode. Together they remove about 4% of the millicode (fpu.c, the softfloat tests) and 12% of program-mode code, which also runs about 17% fewer instructions. - Loop-invariant code motion. Once the rest has settled, and again after legalization (so materialized constants and lui address halves move too): pure values whose operands are all defined outside a loop move to its preheader (the one outside predecessor, or a new block on that edge), innermost loops first. uisa ALU operations never fault, so a value the loop might not have computed is safe to compute early; loads and state reads stay. Hoisting stops when a loop's estimated pressure (SSA liveness) reaches the register budget. Program mode leaves loops that call alone (a value live across the call needs a callee-saved register, and its save and restore cost more code than the hoist saves). Millicode logs every hoist; when a function, with what it calls, then exceeds the registers, its hoists go back to the top of their loop headers before allocation (-v reports it). Program mode runs about 15% fewer instructions with code size unchanged. - Code hoisting. When every successor of a branch is reached only from it and all of them compute the same pure value from operands available at the branch, the value is computed once before the branch. In program mode the same applies after legalization to constants (not in millicode, for the reason constants are only merged within a block). - Tail merging. On the final assembly, after allocation, where identical text is identical work: two blocks that end in the same instructions and continue to the same place (the same jump target or fall-through label, or the same return or no-return instruction) keep one copy, and the other jumps into it. Then branches to blocks that only jump go straight to the destination, jumps to the next label disappear, and blocks nothing reaches are deleted. A bx jump table is never touched. It trades a jump executed on the merged path for the instructions saved. - Out of SSA. Critical edges are split; phis become parallel copies on the incoming edge. A cycle of three or more copies goes through a scratch register when one is free on that edge (one the function or its callees already write, so callers never keep a value there across the call): k + 1 moves for k copies. Two-copy cycles, and cycles with no free register, are broken with three-xor swaps. - Immediates and branches. 14-bit ALU immediates (signed for addi/slti, zero-extended for andi/ori/xori), 12-bit memory displacements, 11-bit compare-and-branch displacements: a branch that does not reach becomes the inverted branch around a jal. - Uses of variables that may be unassigned, falling off the end of a non-void function or an entry function, and calling an entry function are errors.

docs.title: Program mode (--program)
docs.text:
ucc --program compiles ordinary C programs (csmith tests, benchmarks) to code that runs on the uisa ISS and the uisa RTL. Millicode mode, the default, is unchanged: same rules, same z3 allocator, byte-identical output.

build/compiler/ucc --program -o prog.s prog.c       # code + data section
python3 compiler/prog/uimage.py prog.s -o prog.hex   # program image
build/prun prog.hex                                  # run on the ISS: "result <x10> steps <n>"
python3 compiler/prog/test_prog.py [N [seed]] [--csmith N]   # differential tests vs the host cc

Pipeline. The front end, SSA construction and SSA cleanups are shared with millicode. Then (progback.cpp): out of SSA first (critical edges split, phis become parallel copies sequentialized before allocation, a cycle through a new temporary); ABI lowering; per function, Chaitin-Briggs graph colouring with iterated register coalescing (George & Appel: conservative Briggs and George coalescing, freezing, optimistic spilling); spilled values get stack slots and short-lived temporaries, and allocation repeats until nothing spills; then the frame is laid out and the code emitted. The recursion and return-stack rules do not apply: calls are jal x1, f and returns jalr x0, x1, 0, with ra saved in the frame, so recursion and call depth are limited only by the stack.

Calling convention.

registers use x0 zero x1 return address (saved in the frame by non-leaf functions) x2 stack pointer (grows down, 8-byte aligned frames) x10-x17 argument words 1-8; x10-x11 result words x3-x7, x10-x17, x28-x30 caller-saved (a call clobbers them) x8, x9, x18-x27 callee-saved (saved and restored when a function uses them) x31 reserved for the emitter (frame offsets beyond the 12-bit displacement)

Argument words past the eighth go on the stack: word 9 at sp + 0 of the caller at the call, word 10 at sp + 4, ... A 64-bit value is two words (low first); a struct its fields' words. A result of more than two words (a large struct) goes through a hidden first argument: the caller passes the address of a frame object and the callee stores the result there.

Frame (from sp after the prologue, upward): outgoing stack arguments; locals in memory (arrays, address-taken variables); spill slots; saved callee-saved registers; saved ra. The incoming stack arguments follow the frame.

Memory map. Everything is in the hidden (physical) space, accessed with ld.*.h / st.*.h; memory is flat and identity-mapped, big-endian:

address 0x00000000 code: _start (sets sp, jal x1, main, halt 0), then the functions 0x00100000 data: every global, initialized (zero where no initializer says otherwise) below 0x00800000 the stack (sp starts at 0x00800000)

Globals are addressed absolutely (lui + displacement), so a global's address is a link-time constant usable in initializers (u32 *p = &g[3];).

Image and entry convention. uimage.py assembles the code with tools/uisa.py and writes a text image: @<byte address> lines start a segment, each following line is one big-endian 32-bit word (# lines are comments). Execution starts at address 0; the program ends with halt 0 and main's return value in x10 (for csmith programs, the checksum). compiler/prog/prun.cc is the reference loader and ISS; it rejects misaligned or out-of-range accesses, guest-space accesses and millicode-only control flow. The instructions used are the uisa base operations, jal, jalr, lui, halt, and the .h loads and stores.

Language additions (program mode only): - Global variables with initializers (constant expressions, including addresses of globals and their elements), static (ignored: one translation unit) and const on aggregates (read-only data is ordinary data). - Pointers (any depth, to integers, structs, pointers and void), &, *, ->, pointer arithmetic scaled by the pointee size, pointer differences, comparisons, casts between pointers and integers. - Arrays (any number of dimensions, of integers, pointers and structs), global and local, with braced initializers (the elements not named are zero); a[i] is *(a + i); arrays decay to pointers; array parameters are pointers. - Array fields in structs (struct s { u16 v[4]; u8 m[2][3]; };, dimensions are integer constant expressions). A struct value carries its arrays: assignment, by-value arguments and results copy every element (a result over 2 words goes through the hidden pointer, so large structs are copied through memory); s.v on its own decays to a pointer as any array does. - sizeof(type), sizeof(type[n]...) and sizeof expr: a u32 constant from program mode's layout (so it differs from the LP64 host for pointers and for structs with 64-bit fields). The operand is not evaluated. - Locals whose address is taken, arrays, structs that contain arrays and braced-initialized locals live in the frame (so do by-value struct parameters that contain arrays); every other local stays in registers. - The comma operator; prototypes (int f(int);); main may take arguments (they are not set). - C's integer keywords and their combinations with LP64 sizes, as on the host: char 8 (signed), short 16, int 32, long and long long 64, signed/unsigned; an L suffix makes a constant 64-bit like LL. So a csmith program means the same thing on the host and on uisa. - Layout: big-endian, natural alignment capped at 4 (64-bit values are two words, high word first), structs padded as C pads them. Pointers are 32 bits. - Intrinsics: only the uisa base operations (no guest registers, flags, memory spaces or millicode control).

Not supported yet: function pointers, unions, floats, bitfields, volatile (csmith is run without unions, bitfields, floats and volatiles), pointers to arrays (int (*p)[4]), string and char literals, varargs.

Tests (compiler/prog/). test_prog.py compiles each program twice: natively with the host cc (host_prog.h provides ucc's type names, -fwrapv) and with ucc --program + uimage.py + prun, and compares the results. Programs: tests/*.c (hand-written: calls and recursion, memory and pointers, spilling, large frames and stack arguments, array fields and sizeof), tests_csmith/*.c (csmith-format), then random programs from gen_prog.py, a csmith-style generator (globals, arrays, structs, pointers to pointers, loops, switch, recursion; UB-free by construction; main returns the CRC of every global). With csmith installed (csmith on PATH or CSMITH=...), --csmith N also runs N csmith programs: both builds are preprocessed with compiler/prog/csmith/csmith.h, a stand-in for csmith's runtime (its safe math names, the CRC, platform_main_end returning the checksum). csmith has no MacPorts port; build it from source without sudo:

git clone https://github.com/csmith-project/csmith ~/code/csmith
cmake -S ~/code/csmith -B ~/code/csmith/build -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=$HOME/code/csmith/local
cmake --build ~/code/csmith/build -j8 && cmake --install ~/code/csmith/build
CSMITH=~/code/csmith/local/bin/csmith python3 compiler/prog/test_prog.py 0 1 --csmith 200

(local, not install: on a case-insensitive file system that name is csmith's INSTALL file.) csmith programs can run for minutes or forever; like csmith's own scripts, the driver skips (and counts) any program that runs longer than 5 s natively or 500M ISS steps.

docs.title: Not done yet
docs.text:
• Allocation at SoftFloat scale. Large loop bodies (hundreds of values in one loop) are only improved piecewise. Splitting such a loop into overlapping windows along its blocks, or pre-coalescing safe copies to shrink it, would let the loop pass settle them too.
  • Scratch memory. Explicit hidden-memory storage (scratch_base) for state larger than the register file; no syntax for it yet.
  • The SoftFloat milestone. 80-bit extended precision for the 68040 FPU is the next real program; it will probably need arrays in scratch memory, and will show whether z3 allocation scales (bitfield.c: 150 values, well under a second).
  • Faults before commits is not checked yet (intro.md says the compiler will check it on SSA).
  • Dead-flag selection of .nf forms, writing results straight into guest registers (__wrg(D2, x + 1) currently computes into an x register and moves), automatic inlining (only inline functions are inlined), calls into hand-written millicode, and pointers or arrays through intrinsics only.
